help.intro: A small set of pronouns talks about people and things without naming them, and you hear them all day: man (one / you / people in general — In Deutschland trinkt man viel Kaffee), jemand (someone) and niemand (no one), etwas (something) and nichts (nothing), alle (everyone, all) and alles (everything). Three things make them German rather than English. man is always singular and takes the er-form of the verb: man sagt, man kann, man muss — and it is the normal way to say 'you' in the general sense. jemand and niemand are singular too (Niemand ist da, not 'are'). And etwas / nichts pair with a capitalised adjective: etwas Neues, nichts Besonderes. They are the words of instructions, signs and small talk — Hier darf man nicht rauchen. Hat jemand meine Brille gesehen? — and without them you cannot say anything general about people or habits.
help.tips[0].title: man = one / you (in general), always singular
help.tips[0].text: man takes the er/sie/es form: man sagt, man kann, man darf, man muss. It never means 'a man' (that is der Mann). Use it for rules, habits and general truths: Hier darf man nicht parken. In Bayern isst man gern Brezeln.
help.tips[0].trap: English 'you' in 'you can't park here' is not du or Sie — it is man. 'Du darfst hier nicht parken' addresses one person; 'Hier darf man nicht parken' states the rule.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: How do you say that in German?
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: In Germany people separate their rubbish.
help.tips[0].check.why: man always takes the er/sie/es form of the verb, so it's man darf.
help.tips[1].title: jemand / niemand — someone / no one, singular
help.tips[1].text: Jemand hat angerufen. Niemand ist zu Hause. Both take a singular verb. In the accusative and dative you will see jemanden / jemandem, niemanden / niemandem — but the bare forms are also common in speech: Ich kenne hier niemand(en).
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: Has anyone seen my glasses? – No, no one.
help.tips[1].check.why: niemand is singular, like jemand, so the verb takes the er-form: niemand weiß.
help.tips[2].title: etwas / nichts — something / nothing, and the capital adjective
help.tips[2].text: Ich möchte etwas trinken. Ich habe nichts gehört. With an adjective the adjective becomes a noun and takes -es: etwas Neues, nichts Besonderes, etwas Schönes. In speech etwas shortens to was: Willst du was essen?
help.tips[2].trap: German has one negative: 'Ich habe nichts gehört', never 'Ich habe nicht nichts gehört'. And 'nichts' is not 'nicht': nicht negates a verb, nichts is a thing.
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: Is there anything new? – No, nothing special.
help.tips[2].examples[1].en: Would you like something to eat?
help.tips[2].check.q: Im Urlaub habe ich etwas ____ erlebt. (something nice)
help.tips[2].check.why: After etwas, an adjective becomes a noun: capital letter and -es — etwas Schönes.
help.tips[3].text: alle = all the people (plural verb): Alle sind da. Alle Kinder spielen. alles = everything (singular): Alles ist fertig. Ich habe alles verstanden. Also: viele (many), einige (some), wenige (few) — plural like alle.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: Is everyone here? – Yes, and everything is ready.
help.tips[3].check.q: Der Koffer ist gepackt. ____ ist fertig.
help.tips[3].check.why: alles means everything and takes a singular verb (ist). alle means all the people and takes sind.
help.tips[4].title: Pairs
help.tips[4].text: jemand ↔ niemand, etwas ↔ nichts, alle ↔ niemand, alles ↔ nichts. Learn the positive with its negative and you have the set.
help.tips[4].examples[0].en: Someone? No one. Something? Nothing. Everyone? No one.
help.tips[4].examples[1].en: Does anyone know anything? – No, no one knows anything.
help.tips[4].check.q: Ist jemand im Büro? – Nein, ____ ist da.
help.tips[4].check.why: jemand pairs with niemand: someone? – no one. nichts is the partner of etwas.
help.table.caption: The indefinite pronouns
help.remember[0]: man = the general you; it takes the er-form and never means der Mann.
help.remember[1]: jemand/niemand and alles are singular; alle is plural.
help.remember[2]: etwas + Adjective with a capital: etwas Neues, nichts Besonderes.
help.context.en: Hello? Is anyone home? – No, no one is answering. Did you hear something? – No, nothing. Maybe everyone is in the garden. – How do you say it again … 'Is anyone there?' Oh, everything is quiet. Then let's go. In this town there's nothing to do in the evening!
help.mistakes[0].why: man is singular and takes the er-form.
help.mistakes[1].why: German uses one negative word: nichts already means "not anything".
help.mistakes[2].why: After etwas / nichts the adjective becomes a noun and takes a capital and -es.
help.hook: Talk about people and things without naming them — man, jemand, niemand, etwas, nichts — the words of signs, rules and small talk.
categories[0].label: Indefinitpronomen
sentences[0].sentence: Hier darf ____ nicht rauchen. (one / you in general)
sentences[0].why: People in general = man — always with the er/sie/es verb form; not English 'man'.
sentences[2].sentence: Ich habe angerufen, aber ____ war zu Hause. (no one)
sentences[2].english: I called, but no one was at home.
sentences[3].english: Would you like something to drink?
sentences[3].why: An unnamed thing is etwas — shortened to was in casual speech.
sentences[4].why: etwas' opposite: nichts — note the s, unlike nicht.
sentences[5].english: On Saturday everyone's coming to the party.
sentences[5].why: All the people: alle — plural, with a plural verb.
sentences[6].why: All the things: alles — singular, es-form verb.
sentences[7].why: After etwas an adjective becomes a capitalised noun with -es: etwas Neues.
sentences[8].english: What are you doing at the weekend? – Nothing special.
sentences[8].why: nichts works the same way: Nichts Besonderes — capital adjective-noun with -es.
sentences[9].english: How do you say 'sorry' in German?
sentences[9].why: How do people say it: man — the all-purpose 'one'.
sentences[11].sentence: In der neuen Stadt kenne ich noch ____. (no one, as object)
sentences[11].english: In the new town I don't know anyone yet.
sentences[11].why: niemand can take case endings: as the object, niemanden.
sentences[12].english: All the children are playing in the garden.
sentences[12].why: alle before a plural noun: Alle Kinder.
sentences[13].english: Did you hear anything? It was so loud.
sentences[14].english: The fridge is empty, we've got nothing to eat.
sentences[14].why: nichts — 'nothing to eat'; nichts never changes its form.
sentences[15].english: In Germany people separate their rubbish.
sentences[15].why: A national habit = man: man trennt den Müll — 'one separates'.
sentences[17].sentence: Ich habe noch mit ____ darüber gesprochen. (no one)
sentences[17].english: I haven't talked to anyone about it yet.
sentences[17].why: mit takes the dative, and niemand follows: niemandem.
sentences[18].sentence: Im Kino darf ____ nicht laut telefonieren. (one / you in general)
sentences[18].english: You mustn't talk loudly on the phone in the cinema.
sentences[18].why: The general rule-subject is man — darf stays in the es-form.
